## Introduction

The **Poisson process** is the canonical continuous-time model for events that
occur randomly and independently in time, such as customer arrivals, insurance
claims or jumps in an asset price. It is a counting process that increases by
one at each event.

:::{.definition data-title="Poisson Process"}

A **Poisson process** with rate $\lambda>0$ is a process $\{N_t;t\geq 0\}$
taking values in $\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ such that

1. $N_0=0$.
2. **Independent increments:** for $0\leq t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$ the increments
   $N_{t_1}-N_{t_0},\ldots,N_{t_n}-N_{t_{n-1}}$ are independent.
3. **Stationary Poisson increments:** for $s<t$,
$$
N_t-N_s\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s)).
$$

:::

In particular $N_t\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda t)$, so
$$
\mathbb{E}[N_t]=\lambda t \quad \& \quad \operatorname{Var}(N_t)=\lambda t,
$$
see [[poisson-distribution]]. The parameter $\lambda$ is the expected number of
events per unit time.

## Infinitesimal Definition

:::{.theorem data-title="Infinitesimal Characterisation"}

A counting process $\{N_t\}$ with $N_0=0$, independent and stationary
increments is a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ if and only if, as
$h\downarrow 0$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(N_{t+h}-N_t=1)=\lambda h+o(h), \quad
\mathbb{P}(N_{t+h}-N_t\geq 2)=o(h).
$$

:::

That is, in a short interval at most one event occurs, with probability
proportional to the length of the interval. This is the building block for the
[[birth-death-processes|birth-death]] and [[jump-processes|jump process]]
generalisations.

## Inter-arrival Times

Let $T_n=\inf\{t:N_t=n\}$ be the $n$-th **arrival time** and
$\tau_n=T_n-T_{n-1}$ the $n$-th **inter-arrival time**, with $T_0=0$.

:::{.theorem data-title="Inter-arrival Times"}

The inter-arrival times $\tau_1,\tau_2,\ldots$ are i.i.d.
$\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ random variables. Consequently
$$
T_n=\sum_{i=1}^n\tau_i\sim\text{Gamma}(n,\lambda).
$$

:::

:::{.proof}

The first arrival occurs after time $t$ if and only if no events occur in
$[0,t]$, so
$$
\mathbb{P}(\tau_1>t)=\mathbb{P}(N_t=0)=e^{-\lambda t},
$$
which is the survival function of an $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ variable.
By independent and stationary increments the process restarts afresh at $T_1$,
so $\tau_2$ is independent of $\tau_1$ with the same law, and so on. The sum of
$n$ i.i.d. exponentials is Gamma distributed.

:::

This gives an equivalent definition: a Poisson process is the counting process
of a renewal sequence with i.i.d. $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ gaps. The
**memoryless property** of the [[exponential-distribution]] is what makes the
process Markov.

## Conditional Distribution of Arrival Times

:::{.theorem data-title="Order Statistics Property"}

Conditional on $N_t=n$, the arrival times $(T_1,\ldots,T_n)$ have the same
distribution as the order statistics of $n$ i.i.d. $\text{Uniform}(0,t)$
random variables.

:::

So given the number of events in $[0,t]$, their locations are uniform and
independent. This is the basis of the simulation of Poisson processes on a
fixed interval: draw $N_t\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda t)$, then place $N_t$
uniform points.

## Superposition and Thinning

:::{.theorem data-title="Superposition"}

If $N^{(1)},N^{(2)}$ are independent Poisson processes with rates
$\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, then $N^{(1)}+N^{(2)}$ is a Poisson process with rate
$\lambda_1+\lambda_2$.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Thinning (Splitting)"}

Let $N$ be a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ and mark each event
independently as type 1 with probability $p$ and type 2 with probability $1-p$.
Then the type 1 and type 2 events form **independent** Poisson processes with
rates $p\lambda$ and $(1-p)\lambda$.

:::

Thinning with a time-dependent retention probability $p(t)$ is used to simulate
the non-homogeneous processes below.

## Poisson Process as a Markov Chain

$\{N_t\}$ is a continuous-time [[markov-process]] on $\mathbb{N}_0$, in fact a
pure birth process with constant birth rate $\lambda_i=\lambda$ and
$\mu_i=0$. Its generator (rate matrix) has entries
$$
q_{i,i+1}=\lambda, \quad q_{i,i}=-\lambda, \quad q_{i,j}=0 \text{ otherwise},
$$
and the transition probabilities are
$$
p_{ij}(t)=\frac{(\lambda t)^{j-i}e^{-\lambda t}}{(j-i)!}, \quad j\geq i.
$$

The Kolmogorov forward equations $p_{0n}'(t)=\lambda\big(p_{0,n-1}(t)-p_{0n}(t)\big)$
are solved by the Poisson pmf. The process is regular since the holding times
$\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ sum to infinity, see
[[jump-process-stability-regularity]].

## Compensated Poisson Process

:::{.theorem data-title="Compensated Poisson Process"}

The **compensated process** $\tilde N_t=N_t-\lambda t$ is a martingale with
$$
\mathbb{E}[\tilde N_t]=0, \quad \operatorname{Var}(\tilde N_t)=\lambda t,
$$
and so is $\tilde N_t^2-\lambda t$.

:::

:::{.proof}

For $s<t$, by independent increments
$$
\mathbb{E}[N_t-\lambda t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
=N_s+\lambda(t-s)-\lambda t=N_s-\lambda s.
$$

:::

## Generalisations

**Non-homogeneous Poisson process.** The rate is a deterministic function
$\lambda(t)$ and
$$
N_t-N_s\sim\text{Poisson}\left(\int_s^t\lambda(u)\,du\right).
$$
Increments remain independent but are no longer stationary.

**Compound Poisson process.** Each event carries an i.i.d. jump size $Y_i$,
$$
X_t=\sum_{i=1}^{N_t}Y_i,
$$
see [[compound-poisson-distribution]]. This is the simplest Lévy jump process
and is used for insurance claims and jump-diffusion models.

**Cox (doubly stochastic) process.** The rate $\lambda_t$ is itself a random
process, giving over-dispersion ($\operatorname{Var}(N_t)>\mathbb{E}[N_t]$).

## Simulation

:::{.example data-title="Simulating a Poisson Process"}

Using the inter-arrival representation:

::: {#16e3456a .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
lam, T = 3.0, 5.0

# Exponential gaps until time T is exceeded
gaps = rng.exponential(1 / lam, size=int(5 * lam * T))
arrivals = np.cumsum(gaps)
arrivals = arrivals[arrivals <= T]

plt.step(np.r_[0, arrivals, T], np.r_[0, np.arange(1, len(arrivals) + 1),
         len(arrivals)], where="post")
plt.plot([0, T], [0, lam * T], "k--", label=r"$\lambda t$")
plt.xlabel("$t$")
plt.ylabel("$N_t$")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```
